headlines.article_text: JPMorgan blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from account access Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of rogue agents operating at scale and said the bank is building defensive tools. The bank is piloting Smart Cash, an internal tool to forecast cash flow and move funds to maximize yield. Dimon said customers using outside agents must understand the risks and potential transfer of responsibility. In this article JPM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan, and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta. Getty Images JPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. "We're not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts on the bank's third-quarter earnings call. "You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face's servers. The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank's security concerns against tech firms' demands for access. A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers. "Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials and logging in on their behalf," the spokeswoman said. "We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely," she added. That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, such as customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user's credentials. But they can't send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful. There's no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added. 'Liability transfer' Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank's approach, he said, isn't about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely. In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user's cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents. Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," Dimon said. "They should understand there's a liability transfer." Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user's behalf, for example. Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month. In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta's Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren't allowed to operate freely with customers' accounts. headlines.title: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion over money-laundering violations
headlines.summary: The action by the Treasury Department was announced less than a day before Bank of America reports quarterly earnings.
headlines.article_text: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion over money-laundering violations Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The Treasury Department announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. Bank of America admits willfully violating Bank Secrecy Act regulations and failing to "timely report" more than $5 billion in "suspicious" transactions, Treasury said. Treasury's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency imposed a record $750 million civil money penalty against the bank, which counts toward the $1.2 billion total. Treasury separately announced an $11.6 million settlement over sanctions violations. In this article BAC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A Bank of America branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Bank of America was hit with more than $1.2 billion in federal penalties Tuesday after regulators said the nation's second-largest bank failed for years to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions and fix longstanding anti-money-laundering problems. More than $1 billion of the unreported activity involved national security and other high-priority risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity tied to the southwest border, Treasury said in a press release . The action also lands less than a day before the bank reports quarterly earnings Wednesday morning. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which enforces anti-money-laundering rules, said the $1.2 billion penalty is the third-largest in Treasury history. Treasury separately announced an $11.6 million settlement over sanctions violations. Bank of America Corp. stock price As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money-laundering program, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, according to Treasury. "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the press release. Bank of America said in a statement to CNBC that the bank has invested billions in compliance and is "far along" in remediation efforts. The bank said the penalties will result in a $1.2 billion non-tax-deductible charge in its third-quarter results, reducing net income by about 17 cents per share. It said remediation costs are already reflected in its current expense base. "Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," spokesperson Christa Robinson said. The bank's stock was down about 2% in after-hours trading on the news. The new penalties will put renewed focus on the record of longtime CEO Brian Moynihan , who took over in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure resolving tens of billions of dollars in mortgage-related legal and regulatory matters tied largely to decisions made before he became CEO. For much of the past decade, Moynihan has emphasized what he calls "responsible growth," as Bank of America sought to distance itself from the risk-taking and legal problems that followed the 2008 financial crisis . Moynihan is scheduled to appear on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " at 10:20 a.m. ET Wednesday following the bank's earnings report. Treasury says BofA "prioritized its revenues" Treasury said the bank "prioritized its revenues" while minimizing the impact on compliance resources. The agency said the bank relied so heavily on law-enforcement inquiries and referrals from other financial institutions that regulators said it effectively outsourced part of its responsibility for detecting suspicious activity. The penalty from Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network came in coordination with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, or OCC, an independent bureau within the department, which announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America. That sum, which is credited as part of the $1.21 billion total, is the largest penalty OCC has ever levied , the office said. The office accused the bank of serious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering rules, and of failing to fix its deficiencies in accordance with a cease-and-desist order it signed in 2024. "Despite its obligation to the American people as a national-chartered, global systemically important bank, the bank's BSA/AML compliance program continues to reflect widespread breakdowns in internal controls, which threatens U.S. national and economic security," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said in the OCC press release. "The bank's poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable. The second largest bank's egregious and continued BSA violations warrant the OCC imposing its largest [civil money penalty] ever assessed against a bank," Gould said. "The OCC expects all banks to have an effective BSA/AML compliance program. Those that do not can expect swift and significant action from the OCC." The 2024 order had identified a "breakdown" in Bank of America's systems for detecting and reporting suspicious activity, including a "systemic failure" to set appropriate thresholds for triggering investigations. It also said the bank had failed to make "acceptable substantial progress" correcting an earlier customer due diligence problem. Treasury said the failures included red flags involving possible narcotics-trafficking proceeds, fraud and potential trade-based money laundering that were not addressed in a timely way. Bank of America will also be required to conduct a third-party review for suspicious transactions that went undetected and undergo independent reviews of its transaction-monitoring and customer due-diligence programs, Treasury said. – CNBC's Hugh Son contributed to this report. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty Images Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC on Tuesday. The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers at a time when many other employers are offsetting rising healthcare costs with higher prices and scaled-back plan benefits. The announcement comes weeks before open enrollment for Walmart employees closes on Nov. 6. Walmart, the biggest private employer in the U.S., will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Eli Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization. But the company still does not cover GLP-1s from Novo and Lilly for the purpose of weight loss. Other large employers similarly don't cover those treatments for obesity or have recently dropped coverage to tamp down on their healthcare costs. The latest benefit changes build on Walmart's yearslong effort to boost employee compensation after previously receiving criticism for the healthcare benefits and wages it offers. Walmart employs roughly 2.1 million associates worldwide, with about 1.6 million of those workers based in the U.S., as of the end of fiscal year 2026. In a statement, the company said it's minimizing premium increases for its employees, raising rates for its starting plan by $1.50 per pay period to $39.80. Walmart told CNBC that's a smaller increase than the company made last year. The company is also expanding an existing benefit that pays for employees to see cancer specialists at the Mayo Clinic or the Cleveland Clinic, according to a Tuesday letter to workers from Donna Morris, Walmart's chief people officer. Starting next year, employees under most plans can use that benefit to get a second opinion from a specialist for rare conditions such as ALS, multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's. Among the other added benefits is up to 12 weeks of neonatal intensive care unit leave for parents, which can be added on top of regular parental and maternity leave, the letter said. "The steps we're taking are based on years of planning and trying new things, which is allowing us to make meaningful improvements for associates without slashing benefits or significantly raising premiums," Walmart said in its statement to CNBC. headlines.article_text: Micron sinks, other memory-linked names dip for a second day Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Memory-linked stocks fell on Tuesday after Asian and European markets were roiled. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress on a new chip structure, intensifying chip competition. Intel and Broadcom CEOs have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom. In this article SFTBY ASML STM IFX-DE SKHY Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images Memory-linked stocks fell on Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition. Memory chip giant Micron slipped 3.62% while other memory-related names such as SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital also dipped. The slide, which followed declines on Wall Street on Monday, comes as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT . Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to the likes of Micron and South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics . Analysts broadly see CXMT as trailing the U.S. and South Korean memory leaders, which means any advancement from the Chinese firm could add more competition to the market leaders. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. CXMT shares closed 2.8% lower in Shanghai. Micron, Seagate, SanDisk, Western Digital stock chart. 'Vulnerable' AI sentiment? Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks. watch now VIDEO 4:30 04:30 Tech shakedown spreads as U.S. heavyweights face fresh selling Squawk Box Europe Global tech stocks slump Adding fuel to the sell-off was a post by Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, who said China has the ability to scale production once it figures out how to manufacture something. "When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined," Musk said on Monday. European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open. Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.4% — both hitting their lowest levels since August. SK Hynix's U.S.-listed stock was down around 5% in premarket trading. In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry through its huge investment in OpenAI, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. headlines.article_text: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub to showcase Siri AI Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple announced the new HomeView that starts at $299. The iPhone maker also announced the new Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini. HomeView will act as a voice-controlled smart home hub for Apple devices and was built to showcase new Siri AI abilities. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:47 03:47 Apple announces new home products: Here's what you need to know TechCheck Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September. Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under Ternus, who was the company's longtime hardware boss before being promoted to CEO. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music. Apple's HomeView can be placed on a table or mounted on a wall. Apple "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus. "Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home. The Apple HomeView, an iPad-like device meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops that will showcase its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant, during a launch of smart home products in New York City, US, October 13, 2026. Shannon Stapleton | Reuters Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it. Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers. "They are going above and beyond what a lot of other companies do when it comes to privacy and security protections," Kent said. Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales, but also helps further lock customers into its ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone. HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house. Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone. The next generation of the HomePod mini with support for Siri AI Apple Home Collection, part of Apple HomeView which includes an iPad-like device meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops that will showcase its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant, during a launch of smart home products in New York City, US, October 13, 2026. Shannon Stapleton | Reuters Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories.
